opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, because the landscape has changed so much since I started working on simulation.

If I were starting from scratch today, the first thing I'd ask is: who is this simulator for, and what does "good" mean for them? A simulator for visual effects in film, a simulator for robotics training, and a simulator for engineering analysis have very different priorities. In graphics you care about visual plausibility and artist control; in robotics you might care about throughput, millions of steps per second for reinforcement learning, and maybe differentiability; in engineering you care about accuracy and convergence guarantees. A lot of projects go wrong by trying to be everything at once.

Second, I'd think very carefully about the programming abstraction, because that's where I've seen the biggest productivity gap. When I was doing my PhD, writing a high-performance simulator meant juggling CUDA kernels, memory layouts, sparse data structures, and the physics itself all at the same time. You'd spend maybe 10% of your time on the actual physics and 90% on engineering. That's what motivated Taichi: separating the *what* of the computation from the *how*, so the researcher writes something close to the math, and the compiler handles parallelization, data layout, sparsity, and even automatic differentiation. I still believe in that principle. Today I'd also take seriously JAX, Warp, and similar tools, so it's less about inventing a new language and more about picking the right level of abstraction for your team.

Third, I'd design for differentiability from day one if there's any chance you'll want it. Retrofitting gradients into a simulator that wasn't built for them is painful. Differentiable physics opens up system identification, control optimization, and coupling with learning in a really natural way.

Fourth, and this matters more now than a few years ago, I'd think about how the simulator fits with machine learning. There's real excitement about learned simulators and world models, and I think they're genuinely useful, but I don't think they replace classical numerical methods. Physics gives you conservation laws, stability, and generalization outside your training data. The interesting design space is hybrid: use numerical methods for the core dynamics, use learning for the parts that are hard to model from first principles, like complex contact, material parameters, or closing the sim-to-real gap.

And finally, very practically: start simple and get something running end-to-end fast. Pick a robust method over a fancy one. For many problems, something like MPM or position-based approaches gets you surprisingly far with good stability. Build good visualization tools early, because you debug simulators with your eyes. Then profile and optimize only where it matters.

So in short: be clear about your users, choose an abstraction that lets you focus on physics, plan for differentiability, embrace learning where it helps, and iterate quickly.

r001.rationale: The response recommends numerical methods for core dynamics and learning only for selected difficult components, rather than making learning the primary driver instead of Newtonian laws.

r002.rationale: It discusses physics, stability, and generalization, but does not say that approximations should lie in modeled conditions rather than in physical laws.

r003.rationale: The response does not propose object permanence as a constraint in a learned simulator.

r004.rationale: It mentions contact as a potential use for learning, but does not propose a constraint preventing two objects from occupying the same position.

r005.rationale: The response does not propose learning physical dynamics from video or avoiding per-object physical-state sensors.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The honest answer is that I'd start somewhere very different from where I started with Taichi ten years ago.

Back then the hard problem was performance. You had the physics in your head, say a material point method solver, and the bottleneck was getting it to run fast on a GPU without writing thousands of lines of CUDA. So Taichi was really a compiler project disguised as a graphics project. Sparse data structures, differentiable kernels, decoupling the algorithm from the memory layout. That mattered a lot in 2019.

If I were starting today, I'd ask a different first question: who is this simulator for, and what does the data look like coming out of it? Because the biggest consumers of physical simulation now are not film studios. They're people training robots, training world models, generating synthetic data at scale. That changes almost every design decision.

Concretely, a few things I'd do differently.

First, I'd design for throughput across thousands of parallel scenes rather than for one beautiful high-resolution scene. Batch everything from day one. A robot learning policy doesn't care about a single gorgeous splash. It cares about ten thousand mediocre splashes per second with slightly different parameters.

Second, differentiability wouldn't be a feature bolted on later. It would be the default. Every contact model, every constraint solver, I'd write with the gradient path in mind, even if that means picking a slightly softer or slightly less physically pure formulation. A simulator you can't backprop through is only half useful today.

Third, I'd be much more pragmatic about the stack. In 2018 you had to build your own compiler because nothing existed. Now you have JAX, Warp, Triton, PyTorch all generating decent GPU code. I'd stand on those and spend my effort on the physics and the interfaces, not on reinventing code generation. That's a bit humbling for someone who wrote a DSL, but it's the right call.

Fourth, and this is the one people underestimate, I'd think about the simulator as a data engine, not a visualization tool. The output should be structured: trajectories, contact events, rendered observations, all aligned, all exportable in formats learning pipelines want. The rendering and the physics should be one system with shared state, because the thing people actually want is sensor data that matches the dynamics.

And then there's the question of whether you even need a classical simulator anymore, with learned world models getting better. My view is you need both. The classical sim gives you ground truth and controllable counterfactuals. The learned model gives you speed and coverage of messy real-world phenomena. The interesting architecture is one where they feed each other, where the simulator generates training data for the world model and the world model fills in what the simulator can't model well, like deformable objects with unknown materials.

So the short version: start from the consumer, batch and differentiate from the first commit, borrow the compiler, and treat it as infrastructure for learning rather than as a rendering tool. The physics is still the fun part. It's just no longer the whole project.

astra-6.text:
I would start by asking what the simulator is for. Are you trying to make something look convincing, predict a real experiment, or train a robot? Those goals lead to quite different choices about accuracy, speed, and even which physics you need to model.

Then I would build the simplest version that captures the behavior I care about. Pick a numerical method, implement a small example, and check it against a case where you know the answer. Before making it fast, you want to understand whether it is actually solving the right problem.

I would also think about parallel computation early. Simulation gives you a lot of opportunities to use GPUs, but your data structures and memory access patterns matter a great deal. You want an implementation where you can experiment with the physics without rewriting all the performance machinery each time.

So my approach would be to keep that loop short: build a small model, validate it, measure performance, and then add complexity where the application actually needs it.

r001.rationale: It discusses choosing numerical methods and models based on the simulator’s purpose, but does not make learning primary or contrast it with Newtonian laws.

r002.rationale: It recommends validating a model, but does not say that approximation may lie in modeled conditions rather than in the physical laws.

r003.rationale: It proposes building and validating a simple model, without mentioning object permanence as a constraint.

r004.rationale: It does not mention the constraint that two objects cannot occupy the same position.

r005.rationale: It does not propose learning dynamics from video or contrast that with measuring object states using sensors.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d start by asking what we want to simulate and what we need the simulator to do. Is it a tool for predicting physical behavior, generating realistic animation, or training a robot? Those goals lead to different choices about accuracy, speed, and which details matter.

Then I’d build the simplest version that captures the important physics. Pick a numerical method, get a small example working, and check it against something we understand. I’d want that foundation to be correct before adding complexity.

I’d also think about the hardware early. Simulation involves a lot of parallel computation, so how you organize the data and computation can make a big difference on a GPU. But I’d keep the implementation easy to experiment with, because you’re going to change your models and algorithms as you learn.

So my approach would be an iterative one: build a small, understandable simulator, validate it, measure where the time goes, and expand it around the application.
